body:
Why the transition changes skill requirements

Moving towards cleaner production and more efficient resource use can change the tasks performed by workers. Some occupations are newly created; others continue but require additional knowledge. For example, an electrician may need training in photovoltaic systems, while a vehicle mechanic may need new skills to service electric vehicles safely.

Green skills are the knowledge, practical abilities and attitudes needed to perform work in ways that support environmental sustainability.

Different kinds of green skills

  • Technical skills: Installing and maintaining renewable-energy equipment, improving industrial efficiency, treating wastewater and managing materials safely.
  • Resource-management skills: Measuring energy or water use, recognising unnecessary losses and adopting conservation practices.
  • General workplace skills: Problem-solving, teamwork, safe working practices and adapting to new processes.
  • Conservation and livelihood skills: Managing natural resources, restoring ecosystems and carrying out sustainable agriculture or forestry activities.

Not every worker requires a completely new occupation. Upskilling improves or extends skills needed in an existing occupation, whereas reskilling prepares a worker for substantially different tasks or employment.

What is a transition risk?

A transition risk arises when policies, technologies, markets or public preferences change as the economy moves towards lower emissions and greater environmental sustainability.

For example, declining demand for a carbon-intensive technology may affect the businesses and workers associated with it. Equipment can lose economic value before the end of its expected useful life. Such equipment is sometimes called a stranded asset.

RiskSourcePossible consequence
Technology transitionAdoption of cleaner production methodsSome existing skills become less useful.
Market transitionChanges in demand for products and energyEmployment and income may shift between sectors.
Policy transitionNew environmental standards or incentivesBusinesses may face adjustment costs.
Physical climate riskHeat, floods, storms or droughtsWorkplaces, assets and livelihoods may be damaged.

Physical climate risks and transition risks are related but distinct. The first arise from climate-related hazards; the second arise from changes made in response to environmental and economic challenges.

Just transition: protecting people during structural change

A just transition seeks to make the shift towards an environmentally sustainable economy fair and inclusive, while creating decent work and addressing the difficulties faced by affected workers and communities.

A low-carbon technology may create jobs in one location while reducing employment elsewhere. Workers who lose their previous jobs may not have the required qualifications, financial resources or ability to move to the new workplaces. Therefore, the creation of jobs in the economy as a whole does not guarantee that displaced workers will immediately obtain suitable employment.

Measures supporting a just transition include vocational education, reskilling, employment services, social protection, occupational safety, support for affected communities and consultation among governments, employers and workers. The ILO calls such consultation social dialogue.

Employment quality and inclusion

Women, informal workers, low-income households and people in regions dependent on a single industry may face particular barriers to new employment opportunities. These barriers can include lack of training, unequal access to finance, unsafe workplaces or limited mobility.

Inclusive policies seek to remove such barriers. For example, an environmental training programme has a stronger social outcome when it also provides realistic access to employment, safe working conditions and opportunities for disadvantaged learners.

Environmental improvement and employment protection are therefore not competing definitions of a green economy. Both belong within its broader objectives.

Prelims focus

  • Upskilling extends skills for current work; reskilling prepares workers for different tasks or occupations.
  • Transition risks arise from changes in technology, markets and policy during economic transformation.
  • Physical climate risks arise from hazards such as floods, heat and droughts.
  • The ILO adopted guidelines for a just transition in November 2015.
  • Just-transition measures include skills development, social protection and social dialogue.
  • Trap: Growth in total green employment does not guarantee that every displaced worker receives a new job.

[References: ILO, Guidelines for a just transition towards environmentally sustainable economies and societies for all, adopted 5 November 2015, sections on skills, social protection and social dialogue; ILO, What is a green job?, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 7, Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues.]

pictures.caption: Training and worker protection help connect environmental change with decent employment.

title: Green Skills, Transition Risks and a Just Transition

body:
Meaning of natural capital

Natural capital refers to stocks of natural resources and environmental assets, including ecosystems, that provide benefits to people and support economic and social activity.

Natural capital includes forests, soil, freshwater resources, mineral deposits, fisheries, wetlands and other environmental assets. Some are living or depend on ecological processes, while others are non-living resources.

The word capital is used because an environmental asset can provide benefits over time. It does not mean that every part of nature is privately owned, commercially traded or fully measurable in money.

Stock and flow: the central distinction

A stock is the quantity or condition of an asset at a particular time. A flow is something supplied, used or changed over a period.

For example, a forest is a natural-capital asset. The timber harvested during a year is a flow associated with that asset. The forest may also contribute to water regulation, carbon retention and recreation without being cut down.

Similarly, groundwater stored in an aquifer is a stock, while water withdrawn during a year is a flow. A resource may be renewable over time, but it can still be depleted when withdrawals persistently exceed replenishment.

Natural-capital stockPossible flow or contributionRisk to the stock
Forest ecosystemTimber provision, water regulation and recreationClearing, fragmentation and degradation
Groundwater resourceWater withdrawn for usePersistent over-extraction
Coastal mangrove ecosystemCoastal protection and support for fisheriesHabitat destruction and pollution
Mineral depositMinerals extracted for productionDepletion through extraction

Ecosystems and the services they provide

An ecosystem consists of living organisms interacting with one another and with non-living components of their environment. Ecosystem processes such as photosynthesis, decomposition and nutrient cycling maintain the functioning of ecosystems.

Ecosystem services are contributions of ecosystems to benefits used or experienced by people. For example, a wetland may contribute to water purification, a forest may help regulate water flows, and insects may contribute to crop pollination.

Categories of ecosystem services

The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 widely popularised 4 categories:

  • Provisioning services: Material benefits such as food, timber and freshwater.
  • Regulating services: Contributions such as climate regulation, flood moderation, pollination and water purification.
  • Cultural services: Recreational, educational, aesthetic and other non-material benefits.
  • Supporting services: Ecological processes such as nutrient cycling and primary production that help maintain other services.

The more recent System of Environmental-Economic Accounting—Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA) uses 3 broad service categories: provisioning, regulating and maintenance, and cultural. It distinguishes the ecosystem contributions used by people from the underlying ecological processes that help generate those contributions.

This distinction matters when assigning monetary values. For example, the value of an ecological process that supports crop production must not simply be added again to the full value of the resulting crop if doing so counts the same benefit twice.

Ecological condition is as important as area

Two forests may cover the same area but differ greatly in biodiversity, vegetation condition, soil quality and capacity to provide ecosystem services. Similarly, a polluted wetland can retain much of its mapped area while losing important ecological functions.

Major threats to natural capital include habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, pollution, invasive alien species and climate change. These pressures can reduce both the quantity of an asset and the services it supplies.

Prelims focus

  • Natural capital refers to environmental assets or stocks; ecosystem services are flows of contributions associated with ecosystems.
  • The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 used 4 broad ecosystem-service categories.
  • SEEA EA uses provisioning, regulating and maintenance, and cultural service categories.
  • Forest area and forest condition are different characteristics.
  • Trap: An ecosystem's contribution cannot be measured only by the market value of products extracted from it.

[References: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 14, Ecosystem, sections 14.1, 14.7 and 14.8; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation, sections 15.1 and 15.2; Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, Ecosystems and Human Well-being, 2005, ecosystem-services classification; United Nations, SEEA Ecosystem Accounting, introduction and ecosystem-service classifications, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Natural-capital stocks generate flows of services that benefit people.

title: Natural Capital: Environmental Assets and Ecosystem Services

body:
Why ecosystem valuation is needed

Many benefits supplied by ecosystems are not bought and sold in ordinary markets. A mangrove ecosystem can help protect the coast, a wetland can contribute to water purification, and a forest can provide recreation. These contributions may be economically important even when no direct payment is made for them.

Ecosystem valuation attempts to assess the importance of these contributions. Valuation can use physical measures, monetary measures or both. It can help compare the likely environmental consequences of different land-use and development choices.

Physical measurement and monetary valuation

Physical measurement records an asset or service in its natural unit, such as hectares of wetland, cubic metres of water or tonnes of biomass. It answers questions about quantity and condition without requiring a price.

Monetary valuation expresses an identified contribution in money under specified assumptions. It can help place environmental information alongside conventional economic information, but the resulting figure depends on the method, data and purpose of valuation.

Physical and monetary measures are complementary. A monetary estimate cannot replace information about habitat loss, species decline or water quality.

Principal approaches to monetary valuation

ApproachIllustrative useImportant caution
Market-based informationEstimating the contribution of natural resources to marketed timber or fishThe full selling price also reflects labour, equipment and other inputs.
Avoided-damage approachEstimating damage reduced through coastal protection by an ecosystemThe estimate depends on the damage that would otherwise occur.
Replacement-cost approachConsidering the cost of an engineered alternative to an ecosystem serviceThe alternative must realistically replace the relevant service; cost is not automatically value.
Production-related approachEstimating an ecosystem's contribution to crop production through pollinationThe ecosystem's contribution must be separated from other production inputs.
Travel-cost approachStudying the recreational benefits people receive from visiting a natural areaTravel expenditure is not a direct market price for the ecosystem service.

Travel-cost and other preference-based approaches are often used in broader environmental economic studies. They should not automatically be treated as equivalent to the exchange-value estimates used for monetary accounts under SEEA EA.

Why gross market revenue is not the same as nature's contribution

Suppose fish are sold for a total of 100 monetary units. That amount represents the value of the marketed product, not necessarily the value contributed by the aquatic ecosystem alone. Fishing vessels, equipment, labour and other inputs also contribute to production.

In environmental-economic accounting, care is required to separate the resource or ecosystem contribution from those other inputs. Simply assigning the full selling price to natural capital would overstate its contribution.

Double counting

Double counting occurs when the same economic benefit is included more than once in a valuation total.

For example, ecological processes support plant growth, and plant growth contributes to crop production. Adding an independently estimated value for every intermediate process to the full value of crops can count overlapping benefits repeatedly.

Similarly, the estimated annual value of ecosystem-service flows should not be added directly to the value of the ecosystem asset if the asset value already represents the expected future flows of those services.

Limits of monetary valuation

Money can help compare certain benefits, but it cannot fully express every ecological or social consideration.

  • Missing markets and information: Many ecosystem contributions lack observable prices or complete data.
  • Uncertainty: Future ecological change and the effectiveness of possible substitutes may be difficult to predict.
  • Distribution: An overall value does not show who receives the benefits or who bears the costs.
  • Irreplaceability: The destruction of a unique habitat or an irreversible ecological loss may not be adequately represented by a monetary estimate.
  • Non-use and intrinsic values: People may value nature's continued existence independently of direct use; ecological and ethical importance also extends beyond market exchange.

SEEA monetary ecosystem accounts aim for values consistent with national-accounting concepts. They are not intended to measure every dimension of human welfare or the full intrinsic value of nature. Monetary valuation is also not compulsory for preparing natural-capital accounts.

Prelims focus

  • Physical measurement uses quantities or conditions; monetary valuation expresses identified contributions in money.
  • Market revenue for a natural-resource-based product includes contributions from human and produced inputs.
  • Avoided-damage estimates depend on the losses prevented by an ecosystem.
  • Replacement cost does not automatically equal ecosystem-service value.
  • Double counting occurs when overlapping contributions or benefits are added more than once.
  • Trap: A monetary ecosystem value is not a complete measure of nature's ecological, ethical or cultural importance.

[References: United Nations, SEEA Ecosystem Accounting, sections on ecosystem services, monetary valuation and integrated accounts, consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations SEEA, Monetary Valuation for Ecosystem Services and Assets for Ecosystem Accounting, interim technical guidance, sections on exchange values and valuation methods; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 14, section 14.8, Ecosystem Services.]

pictures.caption: Valuation must distinguish ecological processes, ecosystem services and final benefits.
